transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-30 11:00 PT
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Nora (Redwood AE), James (Redwood SE), Elena (Redwood CSM); Maya (HelioPay CTO), Aaron (Platform Eng), Priya (SRE), Samir (Product)

[00:00] Nora: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about 40 minutes, quick agenda — run through last week's results, talk reserve vs autoscale windows, and finalize who does which bench.
[00:18] Maya: yep, thanks Nora.Aaron's got the traffic export ready so we can walk that through.
[00:25] Aaron: hey, yeah i'll share a link in chat after — quick context, we saw two spikes last month, one on 2026-07-08 and a short one on 07-19, peaks around 4x normal qps for 12 minutes.
[00:37] James: ok that matches what we saw in the pilot logs, p95 latency slipped during the 07-08 spike, p99 jumped more dramatically.
[00:44] Priya: unfortunately those were user-facing incidents so we're trying to avoid that pattern again, we've got a p99 SLA target of 800ms for chat completions.
[00:55] Nora: great, so first question — is HelioPay leaning toward reserved capacity with a small autoscale buffer, or trying to keep mostly dynamic autoscale and rely on burst pools? what tradeoffs matter most?
[01:12] Maya: cost's important — we don't want a huge reserved bill. but reliability beats cost if user facing. plus auditors want deterministic behavior for some flows.
[01:23] Samir: to add, some routes (payments confirmations) are higher priority and we could pin them to a guaranteed pool. other lower-critical routes can be best-effort.
[01:31] James: that's actually a common pattern — Redwood supports route-level routing so you can reserve per-route capacity or set min reserve per model. You can also set burst credits for temporary overprovisioning.
[01:47] Aaron: curious about burst credits — how do they age and how much do they smooth 4x spikes for ~10-15 mins?
[01:55] James: good q. burst credits are modeled as a short-term token bucket on top of the Dedicated pool. if your normal sustained qps buys you X credits, a 4x spike consumes them quickly. We usually recommend a small min-reserve plus burst of ~20-25% for short spikes.
[02:15] Maya: that sounds reasonable. can you show how that affects tail latency in real numbers?
[02:22] James: yeah, we ran a synthetic yesterday — with min-reserve at 60% of typical baseline and a 25% burst buffer, p95 stayed under 400ms, p99 around 720ms during a 10-minute 4x spike, assuming KV cache hit-rate of ~70%.
[02:38] Priya: KV cache hit-rate is a big unknown for us; our payloads sometimes vary by user context so hit rate might be lower, maybe 40-50%.
[02:48] James: that will change things — with a 45% hit-rate the same config produced p99 of ~1.2s in our sim. so hit-rate matters a ton.
[02:57] Aaron: can you explain why hit-rate shifts latency so much?
[03:02] James: sure — KV cache avoids re-computing prefixes and lowers token generation per request, also reduces memory pressure. Misses increase per-token compute and kernel invocation, which increases aggregate queueing. At high concurrency, that queueing magnifies p99.
[03:18] Nora: practical step — James will run two sims: optimistic 70% hit-rate and conservative 45% hit-rate and share the traces.
[03:27] James: yes, i'll do that and include tail-latency percentiles and the effective tokens/sec per GPU.
[03:33] Maya: what's the recommendation for min-reserve sizing? our baseline is around 1200 rps across all routes during business hours.
[03:41] James: if 1200 rps is baseline, we'd map that to tokens/sec given your average tokens per request — do you have that metric?
[03:47] Aaron: average completion is ~150 tokens per request, so around 180k tokens/min.
[03:54] James: ok rough back-of-envelope: with T4/RTX-equivalent gpus (our test configs) one GPU at your model quantization level handles ~60k tokens/min under steady-state; so baseline of 180k would need ~3 GPUs reserved. For headroom and failover i'd recommend setting min-reserve to 3 and allow autoscale to add capacity on demand with a small burst buffer.
[04:17] Priya: that seems low-level — what about pre-warm time and autoscale windowing? we can't accept long cold-starts during spikes.
[04:25] James: autoscale has a warm-up latency: provisioning new GPUs adds some time (usually minutes for blob provisioning) so we recommend keeping a small buffer to avoid relying solely on scale-out for sudden spikes. Two knobs: min-reserve (keeps N GPUs always online) and max-burst (allow short oversubscribe).
[04:41] Nora: also note Redwood's continuous batching reduces per-token overhead so that helps during sustained bursts; but it can't eliminate the kernel startup cost when new nodes come online.
[04:49] Maya: ok — sounds like a hybrid. question: how do cost numbers look between reserving 3 GPUs vs reserving say 4 with smaller burst?
[04:57] Nora: i'll attach the pricing spreadsheet but rough numbers: reserve 4 gives lower autoscale spend but higher committed monthly cost. reserve 3 with bursts means some autoscale charges during spikes. We'll send both scenarios.
[05:08] Samir: we also need to account for different model variants — we might run a smaller quantized model for lower-priority routes. can Redwood route by model variant automatically?
[05:16] James: yes, routing policies can map traffic to model variants by route/label. You can set fallback to a cheaper quantized model when primary is saturated. That also reduces token compute.
[05:28] Priya: in security review, we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs for private deployment. Where are we on that?
[05:35] Elena: we've shared the SOC2/ISO certs in previous emails; for KMS we can integrate customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and provide audit trails. i'll resend the security pack.
[05:46] Maya: we'll need that before a VPC pilot, auditors want explicit KMS policy.
[05:51] Nora: noted, Elena will send.
[05:54] Elena: sending after this call.
[05:56] Aaron: back to capacity — curious about a 'reserve burst pool' approach: allocate a small separate pool that only high-priority routes can draw from, so lower-priority traffic doesn't exhaust the burst. is that possible?
[06:10] James: yes, we support logical pools with per-route quotas and priority lanes. You can reserve a dedicated pool for payments-confirmation route and a shared pool with burst credits for everything else.
[06:21] Samir: are there limits to how many pools we can run? we want to keep ops manageable.
[06:26] James: you can create multiple pools but we typically recommend 2-3 logical pools to balance complexity and isolation.
[06:33] Priya: in the logs you mentioned p99 numbers when cache hit is low — can you provide the raw sample traces? we want to correlate to queuing patterns.
[06:41] James: yes i'll export the traces; they'll include token-timing and queue depth so you can replay.
[06:47] Aaron: ok good. One other thing — does Redwood do any adaptive batching that changes behavior as queue builds? we saw some later-stage batching increase latencies in an earlier vendor test.
[06:58] James: Redwood's continuous batching aims to keep latency consistent; it doesn't create large batching windows in response to momentary queue growth. There is configuration for max-batch-wait and target batch sizes, which we can tune.
[07:12] Nora: quick checkpoint — action items we've assigned: James to run sims and share traces; Nora to send pricing; Elena to resend security pack; HelioPay to share traffic histograms and SLA goals. Anything missing?
[07:25] Maya: one ask — can Redwood run a focused tail-latency test with our exact payloads and a synthetic 4x spike pattern? we want apples-to-apples numbers.
[07:34] James: yes we can run a scoped benchmark if you share payload corpus and auth to hit the test endpoint. We prefer a small set of representative prompts and a CSV of timestamps to replay.
[07:45] Priya: will that require exposing any PII? our corpus has masked IDs but some content might be sensitive.
[07:52] James: we can run the test on your sanitized payloads or you can run the benchmark on a private pilot — both work. For privacy we can also sign an NDA amendment if needed.
[08:03] Maya: keep it simple — we will sanitize and deliver a 2k sample set by Tuesday.
[08:10] Nora: perfect. we'll coordinate offline.
[08:13] Aaron: curious about cost optimization — James mentioned quantization earlier; would running 4-bit quant models reduce GPU counts materially?
[08:22] James: yes quantization can reduce memory footprint and increase effective tokens/sec per GPU, but it may affect quality for some prompts. Redwood Optimize can run a quick eval to compare quality degradation vs cost savings.
[08:36] Samir: would that help tail-latency too or mostly throughput?
[08:40] James: mostly throughput and memory; tail-latency improvement is indirect since you can serve more requests per GPU and reduce queueing. But kernel execution characteristics differ, so we'd test p99 explicitly.
[08:52] Priya: if we do a pilot in VPC, what are connectivity requirements? NAT? peering?
[08:57] Elena: for Private we need peering or VPN; for on-prem we have an appliance option. We'll list exact ports and peering expectations in the security doc.
[09:08] Maya: timeline — if we get security docs next week and we share payloads, when could Redwood run a scoped spike test?
[09:15] James: assuming payloads by 2026-08-04 and minimal setup, we can run tests the week of 2026-08-10.
[09:22] Nora: sounds good.
[09:24] Aaron: one operational question — how do we monitor burst credit consumption and set alerts?
[09:30] James: Console exposes token-level cost & latency, burst credit usage, and per-pool dashboards. We can configure alerts on burst consumption thresholds and queue depth.
[09:39] Priya: can we get an API to pull that into our internal monitoring?
[09:43] James: yep, there's a metrics API and webhook alerts. we'll share API docs.
[09:49] Nora: OK — last few minutes, let's recap and confirm owners.
[09:53] Samir: small ask — include example configs for min-reserve=3, min-reserve=4, and reserve+dedicated small payments pool so execs can see cost/latency tradeoffs.
[10:04] Nora: will do.
[10:06] Maya: and please include the scenario where KV hit-rate is low — show sensitivity.
[10:10] James: yes, two sims will cover hit-rate 70% and 45% as discussed.
[10:15] Aaron: i'll get the traffic histogram and sample corpus into the shared drive.
[10:19] Priya: and i'll confirm the VPC subnets.
[10:22] Nora: thanks everyone. we will follow up in email with the pricing and security pack. next sync in one week unless something urgent comes up.
[10:32] Maya: thanks, bye.

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels merged (e.g., Samir and Aaron overlap), minor ASR errors on acronyms (KV sometimes transcribed as K-V, quantization sometimes q-4), and occasional dropped punctuation.
